statement: A stochastic process (X_t) satisfies the Markov assumption (equivalently, 'has the Markov property') if its future evolution, conditional on the present state, does not depend on its past history. In discrete time, for any t_1 < t_2 < ... < t_n < t_{n+1}: P(X_{t_{n+1}}=x_{n+1} | X_{t_n}=x_n, ..., X_{t_1}=x_1) = P(X_{t_{n+1}}=x_{n+1} | X_{t_n}=x_n), whenever P(X_{t_n}=x_n,...,X_{t_1}=x_1) > 0. The term 'Markov assumption' specifically denotes a model in which this property is taken as given (assumed to hold) rather than derived, as in a hidden Markov model.

symbols.meaning: value of the stochastic process at time t (a random variable)
symbols.dimensions: scalar or vector, state space S

symbols.meaning: an increasing sequence of time indices
realized states corresponding to X_{t_1}, ..., X_{t_{n+1}}
filtration (sigma-algebra representing information up to time s), in the general formulation

properties.property: Memorylessness: the future evolution of the process is independent of its history given the present.
properties.why: This is the defining intuition of the Markov property stated at the outset of the source.

properties.property: The 'Markov assumption' names the modeling choice of positing this property holds for a given process, rather than a fact derived from other premises; hidden Markov models are a named example of such a model.
properties.why: The source explicitly distinguishes the term 'Markov assumption' from 'Markov property' on this basis.

properties.property: Discrete-time form: P(X_{t_{n+1}}=x_{n+1} | X_{t_n}=x_n, ..., X_{t_1}=x_1) = P(X_{t_{n+1}}=x_{n+1} | X_{t_n}=x_n), valid when the conditioning event has positive probability.
properties.why: This is the explicit equation given for the discrete Markov property.

properties.property: General (measure-theoretic) form: for a process adapted to a filtration (F_s), and s < t, P(X_t ∈ A | F_s) = P(X_t ∈ A | X_s) for all measurable A.
properties.why: This generalizes the discrete statement to arbitrary state spaces and index sets, reducing to the discrete case when S is discrete and I = N.

properties.property: Equivalent alternative characterization: F_t and F'_t := sigma(X_s : s >= t) are conditionally independent given X_t, i.e. P(A ∩ B | X_t) = P(A | X_t) P(B | X_t) for A in F_t, B in F'_t.
properties.why: The source lists this as one of several equivalent formulations of the same property, useful for verification in different settings.

assumptions.assumption: In the discrete-time statement, the conditioning event P(X_{t_n}=x_n, ..., X_{t_1}=x_1) > 0 so the conditional probabilities are well defined.
assumptions.breaks_when: The joint event of the observed history has probability zero (e.g., continuous state spaces with point conditioning).

assumptions.assumption: The process is adapted to the filtration (F_s) used to express the general form.
assumptions.breaks_when: X_t is not measurable with respect to F_t, so P(X_t ∈ A | F_s) is not well defined relative to that filtration.

failure_modes.mode: Model misspecification when the true process is not Markov but the Markov assumption is imposed anyway.
failure_modes.signature: Conditioning on additional past states x_1,...,x_{n-1} changes the predicted distribution of X_{t_{n+1}} beyond what conditioning on x_n alone gives, contradicting the assumed equality.
failure_modes.cause: The physical/statistical system has memory beyond the current state (e.g., higher-order dependencies) that the chosen state representation does not capture.

The state X_t as defined omits variables needed to summarize history; augmenting the state (e.g., including recent lags) can restore the Markov property, but this is a modeling fix, not something derivable from the property itself per these sources.
